questions.question: Compare particle arrangement and movement in solids, liquids and gases.
questions.modelAnswer: Solid: closely packed, regular arrangement, vibrate about fixed positions. Liquid: close together, irregular, move past each other. Gas: far apart, random rapid motion.
markingPoints: Solid: closely packed, regular arrangement, vibrate about fixed positions.
Liquid: close together, irregular, move past each other.
Gas: far apart, random rapid motion.
questions.evidenceSource: Particle Model of Matter mastery workbook

questions.subtopic: 3.1 Changes of state and particle model
questions.sourceSubtopic: 3.1 Changes of state and particle model
questions.question: Name the changes of state between solid, liquid and gas.
questions.modelAnswer: Solid→liquid melting. Liquid→solid freezing. Liquid→gas boiling/evaporation. Gas→liquid condensation. Solid→gas sublimation. Gas→solid deposition.
questions.evidenceSource: Particle Model of Matter mastery workbook

questions.subtopic: 3.1 Changes of state and particle model
questions.sourceSubtopic: 3.1 Changes of state and particle model
questions.question: Explain why a change of state is a physical change.
questions.modelAnswer: No new substance forms. The particles remain the same substance. The change is reversible by changing temperature.
markingPoints: The particles remain the same substance.
The change is reversible by changing temperature.
questions.evidenceSource: Particle Model of Matter mastery workbook

questions.question: Define internal energy.
questions.modelAnswer: The total kinetic energy and potential energy of all particles in a system.
markingPoints: The total kinetic energy and potential energy of all particles in a system.
questions.evidenceSource: Particle Model of Matter mastery workbook

questions.question: Explain what happens to particle energy when a substance is heated without changing state.
questions.modelAnswer: Energy enters the internal store. Particles gain kinetic energy. Their mean speed and temperature increase.
markingPoints: Their mean speed and temperature increase.
questions.evidenceSource: Particle Model of Matter mastery workbook

questions.question: Explain why temperature remains constant while a pure substance changes state.
questions.modelAnswer: Transferred energy increases particles’ potential energy by overcoming attractions. It does not increase mean kinetic energy. So temperature does not rise.
markingPoints: Transferred energy increases particles’ potential energy by overcoming attractions.
It does not increase mean kinetic energy.
questions.evidenceSource: Particle Model of Matter mastery workbook

questions.question: Define specific latent heat.
questions.modelAnswer: Energy required to change the state of 1 kg of a substance without changing its temperature.
markingPoints: Energy required to change the state of 1 kg of a substance without changing its temperature.
questions.evidenceSource: Particle Model of Matter mastery workbook

questions.question: Explain how gas particles produce pressure on the walls of a container.
questions.modelAnswer: Particles move randomly. Collide with walls and change momentum. Collisions exert a force per unit area on the walls.
markingPoints: Collide with walls and change momentum.
Collisions exert a force per unit area on the walls.
questions.evidenceSource: Particle Model of Matter mastery workbook

questions.question: Explain why heating a gas in a sealed rigid container increases its pressure.
questions.modelAnswer: Particles gain kinetic energy and move faster. Collisions with walls are more frequent. Each collision has a greater change in momentum/force. Pressure rises.
markingPoints: Particles gain kinetic energy and move faster.
Collisions with walls are more frequent.
Each collision has a greater change in momentum/force.
questions.evidenceSource: Particle Model of Matter mastery workbook

questions.question: Explain why reducing the volume of a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature increases pressure.
questions.modelAnswer: Particles travel a shorter distance between wall collisions. Collision frequency increases. Force per unit area increases.
markingPoints: Particles travel a shorter distance between wall collisions.
questions.evidenceSource: Particle Model of Matter mastery workbook

questions.question: A 2.0 kg block receives 18,000 J and its temperature rises by 15 °C. Calculate its specific heat capacity.
questions.modelAnswer: ΔE = mcΔθ C = ΔE ÷ (mΔθ) C = 18,000 ÷ (2.0 × 15) C = 600 J/kg °C
questions.evidenceSource: Particle Model of Matter mastery workbook

questions.question: Melting 0.50 kg of a solid requires 167,000 J. Calculate its specific latent heat of fusion.
questions.evidenceSource: Particle Model of Matter mastery workbook

questions.question: A trapped gas has volume 60 cm³ at 100 kPa. Its volume is reduced to 40 cm³ at constant temperature. Calculate the new pressure.
questions.modelAnswer: P₁V₁ = p₂V₂ P₂ = p₁V₁ ÷ V₂ P₂ = 100 × 60 ÷ 40 P₂ = 150 kPa
questions.evidenceSource: Particle Model of Matter mastery workbook

questions.subtopic: 3.1 Changes of state and particle model
questions.sourceSubtopic: 3.1 Changes of state and particle model
questions.question: Describe how to determine the density of an irregular solid.
questions.modelAnswer: Measure mass using a balance. Partly fill a measuring cylinder and record initial volume. Fully submerge the object and record final volume. Object volume = final − initial. Density = mass ÷ volume. Remove trapped air and read the meniscus at eye level.
markingPoints: Partly fill a measuring cylinder and record initial volume.
Fully submerge the object and record final volume.
Remove trapped air and read the meniscus at eye level.
questions.evidenceSource: Particle Model of Matter mastery workbook
